FOR SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS DECIDING HOW TO STAFF A ROLE

What does this role actually cost — hired, or contracted?

Enter the same role two ways: a W-2 employee's wage plus the employer taxes, workers' comp, benefits and admin that come with it, and a 1099 contractor's rate for the same hours. See the fully-loaded cost of each, side by side, and the contractor rate at which the two are exactly the same.

Workers' comp premium calculator for the class-rate insurance cost that sits on top of payroll

Home care agency margin calculator for pricing an hourly caregiver bill rate from the loaded wage, payer by payer

Staffing markup calculator for pricing a placement you bill to a client, rather than staff yourself

Compare: this calculator vs. a flat burden-percentage rule of thumb.

Guide: how many weeks into the year does FUTA and SUTA stop accruing?

The role, priced two ways

Defaults are a worked example — a $28/hr full-time role against a $40/hr contractor at the same hours. Replace every rate with your own state's and your own policy's before relying on the result.

      These are the worked example’s figures, not yours yet. Change what is different about your role and press the button.

      Common questions

      Does this calculator tell me whether a worker should be a W-2 employee or a 1099 contractor?

      No. Worker classification is a legal determination under the IRS common-law test (behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship type) and, in many states, a separate and stricter ABC test — getting it wrong carries real back-tax and penalty exposure regardless of which arrangement is cheaper. This tool assumes the classification question is already settled, or is being modelled hypothetically for both arrangements, and answers a narrower question: once you pay for the role either way, which one costs more, and by how much.

      Why is FUTA and SUTA not just a flat percentage of wages?

      Both are charged only on wages up to a wage base — $7,000 federally for FUTA, and a state-set amount for SUTA — so once a role's annual wages clear those bases, the rest of the year's wages owe no more of that particular tax. A full-time role clears both bases early in the year, which is why this calculator applies each rate to the wage base rather than to total annual wages.

      Why are ongoing cost and year-one cost shown separately?

      Recruiting, background checks, and onboarding time are one-time costs. A calculator that folds them into a flat annual rate overstates every year after the first. The ongoing figures are what the role costs every year after the first; the year-one figures add each side's one-time setup cost.

      Where do the default tax and benefit rates come from?

      They are illustrative starting points, not your figures. Employer FICA (7.65%) and the federal FUTA wage base ($7,000) are fixed by federal law; FUTA's net rate, SUTA's rate and wage base, and workers' comp all vary by state and, for workers' comp, by class code — replace them with your own state's rates and your own policy's rate before relying on the result.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. None of the wages, rates, or hours you enter are sent anywhere or stored anywhere but this device. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never any of your numbers.

      Does the break-even rate account for the contractor's own self-employment tax?

      No, and it should not — this calculator answers what the role costs your business, not what a contractor takes home. A contractor's self-employment tax is their own cost of doing business, already reflected (or not) in the hourly rate they quote you; it is not a cost your business pays either way.

      No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it does not determine, and is not evidence toward, whether any worker should be classified as a W-2 employee or a 1099 independent contractor. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every rate against your own state's requirements and a qualified accountant or employment attorney before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

      Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record — export or note down anything you need to keep.

      Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. Your wages, rates, and hours are never uploaded and never appear in a usage count — those are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally. We don't have accounts, tracking cookies, or an analytics vendor.

      Hiring in a classified trade? The workers' comp premium calculator estimates the premium and the audit true-up from your own class rates — nothing uploaded.

      Free and open source. If it saves you a spreadsheet, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-a-flat-burden-percentage.html.text:
← Employee vs. Contractor Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat burden-percentage rule of thumb

"Budget an extra 25% on top of wages" is not a burden rate — it is a single number standing in for a mix of a flat tax, two capped taxes, and a fixed-dollar health plan, none of which scale with wages the same way.

What a flat burden-percentage rule of thumb is

Every hiring guide and small-business forum has a version of it: budget an extra 20%, 25%, or 30% on top of an employee's wages to cover "everything else" — taxes, insurance, benefits. It is easy to remember and easy to apply to any wage, which is exactly why it gets reused for every role regardless of whether that role looks anything like the one the percentage was set on.

The number behind it is usually an average across some mix of roles with different wages and different benefits — and then applied as if it were a fixed rate that holds for every role afterward.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the wage and hours, employer FICA, FUTA and SUTA rates and their wage bases, workers' comp, PTO and holiday accrual, retirement match, health insurance, payroll admin, and one-time onboarding cost, and it adds each one up separately instead of guessing a single percentage — for this role, not an average one.

What a flat burden percentage doesWhat this calculator does instead
Applies the same percentage whether the role is a part-time hire with no benefits or a senior full-time hire with a health plan and retirement match. Itemizes FICA, FUTA, SUTA, workers' comp, PTO, retirement, health insurance and admin from what was entered, so the two roles above come out at different percentages instead of one.
Treats FUTA and SUTA as if they applied to every dollar of wages, all year. Caps FUTA and SUTA at their wage bases, the way the taxes actually work, so a role that clears the base early in the year is not overcharged for the rest of it.
Treats health insurance and payroll admin as if they scaled with wages, so the same dollar plan reads as a bigger or smaller "percentage" purely because the wage changed. Prices health insurance and admin as the fixed dollar amounts entered, so a $500-a-month plan costs $6,000 a year on a $16/hour role and a $55/hour role alike.
Has no line for one-time onboarding, so the cost to start a role reads the same as the cost to keep it running. Reports an ongoing annual figure and a separate year-one figure that adds the one-time onboarding or vetting cost.
Gives a rough budget number, not a number to check a specific role's real burden against. Reports the actual burden percentage for the role you entered, so a flat guess can be scored against real cost before you rely on it.

Three roles, the same flat 25% guess

At this calculator's own defaults for federal FICA (7.65%) and the federal FUTA wage base ($7,000), with a common "budget 25% extra" rule of thumb applied to each role's wages:

RoleThis calculator's actual burdenThe flat 25% guessGap
Part-time, 20 hrs/week at $16/hr, 50 weeks, no health plan12.89% of wages ($18,062.50 total)$20,000.00The flat guess prices $1,937.50 above the real cost.
Full-time, 40 hrs/week at $28/hr, 52 weeks, $500/month health plan — this calculator's own default role26.79% of wages ($73,845.38 total)$72,800.00The flat guess prices $1,045.38 below the real cost.
Senior full-time at $55/hr, 3% retirement match, $800/month health plan27.39% of wages ($145,733.30 total)$143,000.00The flat guess prices $2,733.30 below the real cost.

The flat guess is a fixed 25% of each role's own wages, so it moves with wages the same way a percentage always does — it just never moves with the mix of capped taxes and fixed-dollar benefits underneath it. Run your own role's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat percentage is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied to a role whose tax caps or benefits mix do not match whatever role the percentage was set on, and nothing about a round number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your own state's rates or your own benefits offer; it replaces the arithmetic a flat percentage skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat burden-percentage rule of thumb get the cost wrong?

Because the burden is not one percentage of wages -- it is FICA (a true flat rate), FUTA and SUTA (capped at a wage base, so proportionally smaller for a higher-paid role), workers' comp and PTO (rate-based), and health insurance and admin (fixed dollar amounts that are a bigger share of a lower wage than a higher one). A single flat percentage cannot represent a mix of capped, rate-based, and fixed-dollar items at once, so it is only ever right by coincidence.

Does the flat rule overstate or understate the real cost?

Both, depending on the role. For a part-time role with no health plan, this calculator's own defaults put the real burden at 12.89% of wages -- a flat 25% guess overstates the annual cost by $1,937.50. For a full-time role with a modest health plan, the real burden is 26.79% -- the flat 25% guess understates the annual cost by $1,045.38. For a senior full-time role with a richer benefits package, the real burden is 27.39% -- the flat guess understates it by $2,733.30.

Why is a fixed-dollar cost like health insurance not just a percentage?

Because a $500-a-month health plan is the same $6,000 a year whether the role pays $16/hour or $55/hour, so it is a larger share of a lower wage's total cost and a smaller share of a higher wage's. A flat percentage rule assumes every cost scales with wages, and a fixed-dollar benefit does not.

Why are FUTA and SUTA capped instead of a flat rate on total wages?

Both are charged only on wages up to a wage base -- $7,000 federally for FUTA, and a state-set amount for SUTA -- so once a role's annual wages clear those bases, the rest of the year's wages owe no more of that tax. A full-time role clears both bases early in the year; a part-time or seasonal role earning under the bases pays the rate on its full wages instead, which is the opposite of what a flat percentage assumes.

Does this calculator know the right burden percentage for my role?

No. It has no data on your state's SUTA rate or wage base, your workers' comp class code, or what benefits you offer. It takes FICA, FUTA, SUTA, workers' comp, PTO accrual, retirement match, health insurance, and payroll admin as separate inputs and adds them up for the role you describe -- the itemization a flat percentage skips, not a market survey.

Open the Employee vs. Contractor Cost Calculator to price your own role.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, accounting, or financial advice, and it does not determine, and is not evidence toward, whether any worker should be classified as a W-2 employee or a 1099 independent contractor. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Verify every rate against your own state's requirements and a qualified accountant or employment attorney before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a role.

Free and open source. If it saves you a spreadsheet, the code is under an MIT licence — support via GitHub Sponsors is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

when-does-futa-suta-stop-accruing.html.text:
← Employee vs. Contractor Cost Calculator

How many weeks into the year does FUTA and SUTA stop accruing?

Federal and state unemployment tax is charged only up to a wage base, not on a role's full annual wages, so for a full-time hire, both taxes are typically fully paid within the first two or three months of the year, then owe nothing more until the calendar resets.

Run this on your own numbers

The calculator's own worked example, week by week

This tool opens with a worked example: a $28-an-hour, 40-hour-a-week role, paid for all 52 weeks — $1,120 a week, $58,240 for the year. At the default federal FUTA wage base of $7,000 and a default state SUTA wage base of $9,500, here is when each tax stops accruing:

WeekCumulative wagesFUTA base ($7,000)SUTA base ($9,500)
6$6,720not yet reachednot yet reached
7$7,840crossed this weeknot yet reached
8$8,960already cappednot yet reached
9$10,080already cappedcrossed this week
10-52$11,200-$58,240already cappedalready capped

By week 7 — roughly the second week of February, for a role starting January 1st — the role's cumulative wages have already passed the $7,000 FUTA base, so none of the remaining 45 weeks of wages owe any more federal unemployment tax. By week 9, the same is true of the $9,500 SUTA base used in this example. The role works 43 more weeks that calendar year without adding a cent to either tax.

What that does to the actual dollar amount owed

Because each tax is charged on the wage base, not on the $58,240 in total annual wages, the amounts owed for the whole year are small next to what a flat-percentage guess would suggest: FUTA owed for the year is $42 (0.6% of the $7,000 base), and SUTA owed for the year is $256.50 (2.7% of the $9,500 base). A guess that applies the same two rates to the full $58,240 in annual wages instead — because it never accounted for the cap — would put FUTA at $349.44 and SUTA at $1,572.48, overstating the two taxes by roughly 8x and 6x respectively. Neither error is large next to the role's total cost, but it is exactly the kind of small, wrong-by-a-multiple detail that a flat "budget 25% on top of wages" rule of thumb never surfaces, because it never itemizes far enough to be wrong about a specific line.

Where the crossing point moves

The crossing week moves with the wage, the hours, and the state's own SUTA wage base — none of which this calculator assumes. A higher hourly wage or more hours a week reaches either base sooner; a state with a higher SUTA wage base, such as $15,000, pushes the SUTA crossing point out to week 14 instead of week 9 for the same $1,120-a-week role. A part-time or seasonal role that never accumulates $7,000 or $9,500 in wages within the calendar year never crosses either base at all, and pays the tax rate on its full wages for the whole period it works — the cap only matters once cumulative wages pass it, and a role that stays under both bases never gets the benefit this page describes.

Common questions

How many weeks into the year does FUTA stop accruing on a full-time hire?

For a full-time role earning $1,120 a week (this calculator's own worked example: $28/hour at 40 hours), cumulative wages cross the $7,000 federal FUTA wage base during week 7 — cumulative pay is $6,720 after week 6 and $7,840 after week 7. From that week on, none of the role's remaining wages for the calendar year owe FUTA.

How many weeks into the year does SUTA stop accruing?

It depends on the state's wage base, which this calculator takes as an input rather than assuming. At this tool's default SUTA wage base of $9,500, the same $1,120-a-week role crosses it during week 9 — cumulative pay is $8,960 after week 8 and $10,080 after week 9. A state with a higher wage base, such as $15,000, pushes that crossing point to week 14 instead.

What does a flat percentage-of-annual-wages guess get wrong here?

It charges the FUTA and SUTA rate against the full year's wages instead of against the wage base, which overstates both taxes by several times. At the calculator's defaults, the actual FUTA owed for the year is $42 (0.6% of the $7,000 base) and the actual SUTA owed is $256.50 (2.7% of the $9,500 base) — a flat-rate guess applied to the full $58,240 in annual wages would put FUTA at $349.44 and SUTA at $1,572.48, overstating the two taxes by roughly 8x and 6x.

Does this mean a part-time or seasonal role pays the same way?

No. A role that never reaches the wage base within the calendar year pays FUTA and SUTA on its full wages, with no point at which the tax stops accruing — the cap only matters once a role's cumulative wages pass it, which a full-time role does early and a lower-hours or seasonal role may not do at all.

Does crossing the wage base change what this calculator reports?

Yes, and it already accounts for it: this calculator applies each rate to the lesser of a role's annual wages and its wage base, not to total annual wages, so the annual FUTA and SUTA figures it shows are the capped amount, not a full-year guess.

No warranty. This page is arithmetic on the calculator's own defaults and general federal wage-base rules, not tax advice. FUTA and SUTA rates, wage bases, and effective dates vary by state and by year — verify your own state's current SUTA wage base and rate, and the current FUTA rate, before relying on any figure here. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.
